summary:
Liberia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The offence of sodomy carries one year of imprisonment and applies to women as well as men. The provision is domestic in origin rather than a colonial import, so no external legal framework exerts pressure toward repeal.

No legal gender recognition exists. There is no administrative process by which a trans person can amend the name or gender marker on a Liberian identity document, so a visitor whose papers do not match their presentation holds documentation that cannot be brought into consistency through any official route.

Legislative pressure is active and hostile. On 16 October 2024, Rep. Johnson N. Williams was reported to be seeking fellow lawmakers' support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer, with related proposals that would imprison children as young as ten years old for gay sex. Proposals for longer custodial sentences for homosexuality have circulated before: in 2012 then-Senator Jewel Howard Taylor introduced a bill making same-sex marriage a first-degree felony carrying up to ten years, which passed the Senate but not the House and never became law.

Enforcement of the existing sodomy law is uncommon, but its presence shapes reporting behaviour. LGBTQ Liberians deterred from approaching police include victims of crime, and some individuals have been arrested on the basis of their sexuality or gender identity after attackers invoked that status as a pretext.

Gender-affirming hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery are not available in Liberia, leaving a trans visitor without domestic clinical provision for transition-related care.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised. By contrast, Section 2.4(b)(iii) of the Decent Work Act (2015) entitles anyone seeking to work in Liberia to do so regardless of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation, providing an employment-law protection that no other area of Liberian law matches.

Private spaces where LGBTQ people can be open exist, generally sponsored by advocacy organisations such as Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL) or the Transgender Network of Liberia (TNOL) or created by private individuals, because LGBTQ Liberians frequently conceal their identities in public.
tangentialFactors:
Official rhetoric has reinforced the legal position. In March 2012 President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, defended the laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview, drawing international comment; she had also threatened to veto either of the two anti-LGBTQ bills before her that year. Neither veto nor the international attention changed the statute.

Public hostility surged in 2012 as the United States announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas. New legislation proposing longer jail terms for homosexuality was tabled in that period, and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

A 2013 UN-AIDS survey put HIV/AIDS prevalence among Liberian men who have sex with men at 19.8%, a figure relevant to any health screening a visitor might undergo.

The UNDP and OHCHR published a participatory review of the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia in April 2020, the most recent structured international assessment in the record.
localsOnly:
Employment protection under Section 2.4(b)(iii) of the Decent Work Act (2015) is available to residents, covering sex, gender identity and sexual orientation in access to work. No equivalent statutory protection covers housing, services or public accommodation.

Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL), the first NGO founded by LGBTQ Liberians for LGBTQ people, was established to educate men who have sex with men about HIV/AIDS, test them and counsel those testing positive; since 2012 its services have extended to all LGBTQ people.

Residents report that the rarity of sodomy-law enforcement does not remove the practical barrier to police contact: victims of assault frequently do not report, and LGBTQ status has been used against people by both attackers and arresting officers.

The 2012 marriage felony bill died in the House rather than on a veto, leaving its reintroduction a standing possibility for residents as well as visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not quantify how often the sodomy provision is enforced; the assessment that enforcement is uncommon rests on country-reference coverage rather than prosecutorial statistics, and conviction figures remain unresolved.

The October 2024 bill's subsequent parliamentary stage is not sourced. Whether Rep. Johnson N. Williams secured the support he sought, whether the bill was introduced, referred or defeated, and whether the proposals covering ten-year-olds were formally tabled are all unresolved in this record.

The availability of gender-affirming care is sourced to open-reference country coverage with no date attached; whether any private or outbound provision exists is not established here.

The 2020 UNDP/OHCHR review is cited as a source of record but its specific recommendations are not extracted into this inventory, so its findings on legal reform prospects remain unverified in this entry.

Whether the Decent Work Act non-discrimination clause has been invoked successfully before a Liberian court is not sourced.
